title: Scipio's small bath
hookLine: Seneca visits Scipio's plain country house and its tiny dark bath (Letters 86)

cards: Scipio Africanus was the Roman general who beat Hannibal, the man Seneca calls the terror of Carthage. After all of it, he left Rome for a farm at Liternum, on the coast.
Long afterward, Seneca goes there and stays in Scipio's own house. He looks over the stone walls and the towers, and then he finds the bath. It's tiny, and dark, and he's delighted.
The eighty-sixth letter is a tour, and a little sermon on plumbing.

teach.b: The house is built of squared stone, with a wall around a wood and towers at both ends. Seneca writes lying in the very house of Scipio, and he has paid his respects at what people say is Scipio's tomb.
Then the bath: small, narrow and dark, in the old style. The old Romans, Seneca says, didn't think a bath was warm unless it was dim.
Here the man who terrified Carthage washed a body tired from farm work, under this cheap roof, on this plain floor.

Now, Seneca says, people feel poor unless their walls shine with big precious mirrors, unless their pools are lined with marble, unless water pours from silver taps. In Scipio's bath there were slits rather than windows.
Now people sneer at any bath that doesn't take in the sun all day through huge windows. Seneca isn't telling anyone to bathe in the dark.
His point is that the great man of Rome needed very little, and lost nothing by it.
Looking back on the week, from Attalus's old wine and school in old age to the stage kings, the honest timetable and the bees, the thread is plainness: honest memory, honest days, honest pleasure.

how: Some people inspired by Seneca keep one part of their life deliberately plain, a meal, a room or a routine, and take pleasure in it rather than in upgrades.

games.q: you're staying in a hero's old farmhouse, and the bath is a tiny dark cell. what does Seneca feel?
o: delight: the man who beat Carthage washed here, and it was enough.
games.why: Seneca praises the plain bath and contrasts it with the mirrored, marble baths of his own day.

practice: Choose one plain thing near you, a glass of water, a slice of bread, the light through a window, and give it your full attention, as if it were a hero's bath: its texture, its weight, its use.
Let it be enough for this minute, and if a wish for something fancier rises, let it pass.

wordCard.voice: Balneolum. Latin for a little bath: Scipio Africanus washed in one, narrow and dark, after farm work, and Seneca says it was enough. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: a little bath. Seneca, Letters 86.4, describes Scipio's as narrow and dark in the old style.

carryVoice: Your line: plain was enough. Next week, Seneca on learning and on living together. That's a week of Seneca.
